title: Truth
hook: Pilate asks what truth is and walks out; the Dominicans made the word their motto

segments.voice: Yesterday, the order approved, and the first thing Dominic did was scatter his few friars. Your line was to the cities. What did you send out of your hands? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-three.

A Roman governor, early in the morning, in his own headquarters. A prisoner stands in front of him, hands tied. The prisoner says he came into the world to give testimony to the truth. And the governor, Pilate, answers with a question people still ask at kitchen tables and in philosophy classes. In the Douay-Rheims: "What is truth?" Then John's Gospel adds a detail that's easy to miss. Pilate doesn't wait. He goes straight back outside to the crowd. A question that large, and he walks out on it. Today, an order that decided to stay in the room. Its motto is one word: truth.
screen: `A GOVERNOR, A PRISONER, EARLY MORNING.` → `WHAT IS TRUTH?` → `HE DOESN'T WAIT FOR THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: The word is veritas, Latin for truth, and the Dominicans carry it as their motto. You find it on their crests and over their schools. Start with the Latin Bible, the one a medieval friar read. There, Pilate's question is quid est veritas, what is truth. And here is a word game someone later noticed: rearrange the letters of quid est veritas and you get est vir qui adest. It is the man who is here. The answer was standing in front of Pilate the whole time. That's the Christian claim underneath the motto. In John's Gospel, Jesus says, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life." So for a Dominican, truth isn't only a set of correct statements. It's someone to follow. And truth in this tradition isn't meant to stay private. Jesus promises in John that knowing the truth sets people free: "the truth shall make you free." Free, not cornered. That shapes how the truth gets told. Paul's letter to the Ephesians has a phrase for it: "doing the truth in charity." Truth and charity, held together. Either one alone goes wrong. Truth without charity becomes a weapon. Charity without truth becomes flattery. The order's own history shows how hard it is to keep the two together, and in a few days this path will look at that honestly. But the motto still points at a simple daily task: say what is real, and say it as someone who wants the other person to be free.
screen: `VERITAS: THE DOMINICAN MOTTO.` · `QUID EST VERITAS? EST VIR QUI ADEST.` · `TRUTH IS SOMEONE TO FOLLOW.` · `DOING THE TRUTH IN CHARITY.` · then, large: `THE TRUTH SHALL MAKE YOU FREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell the truth kindly, first in rehearsal. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one true thing you've been avoiding saying to someone. Maybe a worry about a friend. Maybe that you were hurt. Maybe that you were wrong. Don't say it yet. Just find the sentence. Now say it over in your mind, slowly, the way you'd want to hear it if you were them. Take out the sharp edge, keep the truth. Breathe. If you pray, you can ask for the courage and the gentleness together. If not, simply sit with the sentence until it feels both honest and kind. The bell holds the time.
Veritas. Latin for truth, and the Dominican motto: truth that is someone to follow, and truth told in charity. Today's word.
Your line: veritas. Today, say the true sentence you found, or one like it, and say it the way you rehearsed it. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Veritas appears on the shields and in the mottos of Dominican houses, schools and colleges; Dominicans connect it to study, preaching and the belief that Christ is the truth.

notes: Confirm Veritas as the Dominican motto and its use on Dominican shields and schools (stated without 'most' or 'all').
The anagram quid est veritas / est vir qui adest is a traditional medieval word game; the letters check (14 each). Attributed only as 'someone later noticed'. Confirm phrasing.
The hook says 'early in the morning' (John 18:28, 'it was morning') and that Pilate went out again (John 18:38). Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of John 18:38, 14:6, 8:32 and Ephesians 4:15.
The teach points ahead to the Inquisition day (1241) without detail; confirm the forward reference is wanted.
Editor: 'the biggest question in the room' (superlative) softened; John 8:32 quotation trimmed to the clause whose Douay-Rheims punctuation is certain, the rest paraphrased.
